Hashing from the handle rather than a re-read pathname means the bytes pinned are the bytes of the inode opened. The unsupported branch must refuse rather than fall back to os.ReadFile: degrading would silently void the guarantee on exactly the platforms nobody tests, and a caller would pin a symlink target believing it pinned the declared file. The SCOPE limit is stated rather than implied because Codex's P1 on #210 was right — none of this constrains the provider, a separate process doing its own pathname open minutes later, so a peer can swap a component after the check returns. Ralph's guarantee is DETECTION at completion, not prevention; real prevention needs a sandbox/namespace/brokered-FS primitive around the provider and is separate work.

decision: A containment refusal BLOCKS the task (MarkBlockedInput) rather than skipping it; an I/O fault resolving paths surfaces as an error instead.
why: A silently skipped task is indistinguishable from one waiting on a dependency, so the refusal would be invisible to an operator and the plan would look merely slow. Blocking puts the reason in task metadata where the observe surface shows it. The I/O-fault split matters because marking a task permanently blocked for a transient filesystem error would strand it.

decision: The Windows winio Stop deadlock is a REAL recurring failure, not a rare flake — it hit twice within hours (PR #221 and PR #225 runs), both in TestAcquire_SecondFailsWhileFirstHolds, both parked in win32PipeListener.Close.
why: I initially characterized it as rare because main had been green. Two independent occurrences in one afternoon on unrelated PRs refutes that framing and confirms PR #224's ordering fix is load-bearing rather than speculative hardening. Recording the frequency because the ORIGINAL instinct — treat a 10-minute CI timeout as infrastructure noise and re-run — would have left this in place indefinitely.

decision: Exclusive output reservations are an ADMISSION constraint checked inside the claim transaction, not edges in the dependency graph. ClaimTask refuses (ErrOutputReserved); ClaimNextReady skips. ReadyPartitions still reports a reserved task.
why: Two tasks writing the same file are legitimately ready at the same instant — neither consumes the other's result — so an edge between them would be a lie AND would serialize them permanently rather than only while one runs. The check must be inside the claim transaction: a separate query lets two claimers both observe no conflict and both proceed, the exact race reservations prevent. The two claim paths differ deliberately: ClaimTask refuses because the caller named that specific task, while ClaimNextReady skips because a blocked task must not hide the other ready work behind it. Scoping to running holders makes a reservation a lock for the duration of a run rather than a permanent path-to-task assignment. ReadyPartitions keeps reporting a reserved task because it IS ready — hiding it would conflate readiness with admission and make a temporarily-unclaimable task look unsatisfied.

decision: Claude failure classification keys on the result frame's api_error_status, NOT on subtype and NOT on the result prose. Unrecognized statuses stay generic. New durable categories: provider_auth (401/403, non-retryable), provider_throttled (429), provider_unavailable (5xx).
why: Verified against installed claude 2.1.220 rather than assumed, and the capture refuted the assumption: a rejected key emits {"is_error":true,"subtype":"success","api_error_status":401}. subtype says SUCCESS on a hard failure, so subtype-keyed logic reads it as a completed turn; is_error is what makes it a failure and api_error_status is the reliable discriminator. Matching the human-readable `result` field would be unstable across CLI versions AND would drag provider text across the never-scrape boundary, so categories are fixed constants with a test asserting 'Invalid API key' never reaches Ralph's error surface. Unrecognized stays generic because forcing a status into the nearest category sends an operator to fix the wrong thing — worse than saying only that the turn failed. The retry split is operational: retrying an invalid credential burns the retry budget and DELAYS the operator seeing the real problem, while 429/503 is exactly what retries are for.

decision: A real-CLI contract test must drive the CLI DIRECTLY, not through ClaudeRunner, when the suite may itself run inside another agent's pty session.
why: My first probe routed through ClaudeRunner and failed with 'claude exited nonzero: exit status 1' and an EMPTY evidence file — no frame ever written. I nearly recorded that as a classification defect. The sanity check refuted it: a fully VALID, authenticated claude turn fails identically under Ralph's pty from inside this session, so the failure was the nested-pty harness, not the code. The contract worth protecting is the FRAME SHAPE (api_error_status still 401), which a direct exec verifies without a pty. The test comment states this rather than leaving a future reader to rediscover it.

decision: Both user-facing import surfaces route through orch.ImportPlan: supervisor.HandlePlanImport and the CLI's offline fallback. Neither calls CreatePlan+SetPlanStatus.
why: Codex P1 on #221, confirmed: EVERY ImportPlan caller in the repo was a test, so nothing user-facing reached the graph ingress. A plan declaring `after:` edges imported with none of them — user-authored ordering was silently discarded and the plan ran in document order. Routing the OFFLINE fallback too is not optional: otherwise an offline import and an online import of the same file produce different plans, which is the worst kind of inconsistency because it depends on whether a daemon happened to be running.

decision: stepTaskID is the single id rule shared by import and dispatch; the dispatch path claims BY NAME via ClaimTask. parseStepRefID is deleted.
why: Codex P1 on #221, reproduced before fixing. Importing a step annotated {"id":"build"} created task "build"; dispatch then derived its own positional "0.0" and materialized a SECOND task for the same step. The observed end state was both nodes present, "build" marked running with dispatched=0, and the error 'claimed task "build" is not a plan step id' — the task stuck running with no worker launched. Claiming by name matters because letting the store substitute a different ready task pairs one task's row with another's instructions; survivable while ids were positional and the caller could re-derive the step, and a hard bug the moment ids come from metadata since a non-positional id has no StepRef to parse back into.

decision: Acceptance criteria are derived at IMPORT **or at first materialization** (defaultAcceptanceJSON in both paths, since dispatch may materialize a plan that never went through ImportPlan) and persisted in the same transaction as the node.
why: Codex P1 on #221 — a verification-integrity hole, not a cosmetic gap. VerifyAndComplete consults only the stored acceptance_json, and an EMPTY value selects judgment-only verification. So a task whose plan declared `accept: <cmd>` could be completed by non-empty worker evidence alone, never rerunning the command or checking the file the plan demanded. That silently downgrades the orchestrator-verified-completion invariant the whole design rests on.

decision: Removed StatusReply.RepoPath, StatusReply.PID, and WorkerSummary.ProviderSessionID from the CmdStatus wire contract rather than leaving them unpopulated.
why: All three had ZERO production consumers (grep across internal/ and cmd/ found only tests); RepoPath and ProviderSessionID were never populated at all. They describe the supervisor HOST — an absolute filesystem path and an OS process id — not the work an operator watches, and they went to every attached client on every status poll. Leaving a declared-but-unused field on a wire contract is not neutral: it invites a future implementer to fill it in, and the leak then arrives without anyone deciding to add it, which is precisely how RepoPath came to be declared but never set. The four referencing tests asserted round-tripping and 'a degraded reply is still a real reply' — properties about the reply, not these fields — so ActiveWorkers and ProtoVersion carry them now.

decision: A client that PAGINATES then FILTERS must exhaust pagination before filtering, and must restore the command's prior ordering and default status set explicitly rather than inheriting the query endpoint's.
why: Four review findings on the plan-ls rewrite, all regressions I introduced by treating 'route through the supervisor' as a pure transport swap. It is not: the snapshot endpoint has its OWN page cap, ordering (p.id ASC), and status set, and adopting them silently changed operator-visible behavior. Filtering a truncated page is strictly worse than truncating a filtered one — with 200+ plans the command could print 'no plans' while an active plan sat on page two. Ordering by id instead of updated_at DESC means an operator who just paused a plan finds it wherever its id sorts. Including drafts changed the default view with no flag change on the operator's side, while the --all help still described --all as what widens beyond active+paused. And the help text still promised offline queuing after the offline fallback was deliberately removed. General rule: when moving a command behind a query API, the command's contract — ordering, defaults, completeness, help — is the thing to preserve, not the API's.

decision: BLOCKED pending user: `origin` points at the Gitea MIRROR while `github` points at the source of truth, so the default push target is backwards. Not changed unilaterally.
why: Verified every push this session went to github explicitly, and the mirror is healthy — main byte-identical (20c68f04), branch sets identical. The risk is not what I pushed but what an unqualified command would push: git/gh default to `origin`, which is the mirror. Two branches read as diverged only because I force-pushed them today and Gitea still holds pre-rewrite SHAs — lag on rewritten history, not divergence. Renaming changes where an unqualified push lands on a public OSS repo, and the direction of the mirror is not evident from the repo (no mirror workflow in .github/workflows/, implying a Gitea-side pull). Guessing wrong on either point could push the mirror over the source of truth, so this is a real user decision rather than an implementation detail.

decision: vconfig.ConfigSource is the seam between config resolution and its backing store. The supervisor passes a store-backed source, the CLI passes an IPC-backed one, and BOTH run the same resolution code. Values cross the wire as RAW JSON strings; upserts and deletes travel in ONE call; the SUPERVISOR resolves the user-scope project.
why: Taking a *store.Store meant every caller wanting its effective config had to be a direct database reader — the dumb-client violation #204 targets. One seam gives one resolution path instead of a client path and a server path that drift. Raw strings because vconfig owns the encoding and decoding in the supervisor would make it a second interpreter of a schema it has no stake in. One call because vconfig computes upserts and deletes together (an overlay plus, for a provider-selection replacement, a legacy key to remove) and two round trips would let a crash in between leave the project holding both the new selection AND the stale key it replaced. Supervisor-side user-scope resolution because resolving that project may CREATE it, which is a store write and the supervisor is the single writer of record.

decision: NewStoreConfigSource(nil) returns a nil *StoreConfigSource, so callers must use isNilConfigSource rather than `src != nil`.
why: The classic Go typed-nil trap: a nil pointer inside a non-nil interface is NOT == nil, so a plain nil check passes and the next method call panics. That would silently break vconfig's documented 'no store, file layers only' path — which exists for exactly the callers least likely to have a store. Asserted by TestStoreSatisfiesTheSource rather than trusted.

decision: GitHub API rate limit (GraphQL 5000/5000) was exhausted by per-PR review-thread polling in the merge watchers. Future watchers must poll REST (gh pr checks/view) and reserve GraphQL for actual thread reads/mutations.
why: Each watcher round issued one GraphQL reviewThreads query PER open PR, and several watchers ran concurrently over ten PRs. Worse, the exhaustion was SILENT: `gh pr view --json state` returned empty on rate-limit, my `grep -c OPEN` counted zero, and the watcher reported 'ALL MERGED' against a main that had not moved. A watcher must treat an empty API response as unknown rather than as a terminal state — reporting success from a failed query is the same class of error as a test that passes because it never ran.

decision: provider.ResolveInvocation is the single resolution path for all three runners. Result.Invocation reports the CONCRETE model/effort a turn ran as. StrictBinding (off by default) refuses a request the binding cannot honor exactly. Validation is config-driven, NOT a hardcoded per-provider model table.
why: Verified against main before writing: resolveModel treats the sonnet override as a general fallback, so a codex binding configured only with SonnetModel='gpt-5' answers a request for ModelOpus with 'gpt-5' and returns no error — a task pinned to a model runs on a different one and nothing reports it. Reporting the invocation makes provenance reflect reality rather than the request ('opus' in the plan and 'gpt-5' on the command line are both true; only the second explains the result). Strictness defaults OFF because every existing plan relies on loose tier resolution and flipping it would change what those plans run. The archived branch validated against hardcoded per-provider model prefixes and effort lists; that duplicates what BindingConfig already declares and drifts the first time a provider ships a new model, so the binding's own config is the authority. Routing all three runners through one path means strictness cannot be enforced in one runner and skipped in another.

decision: REFUSED claude --permission-mode bypassPermissions and opencode --auto. SHIPPED claude --no-chrome and opencode --pure. Both refusals are enforced by tests, and binding config Args still append last so an operator can opt in per binding.
why: The bypasses were proposed to stop permission prompts blocking a turn, but they are not needed for that: the watchdog already kills a prompting turn and reports FailureInteractivePrompt, so the never-block invariant holds without them. What they WOULD change is the blast radius of an agent running unattended against a real checkout — every gate the CLI would otherwise enforce, gone. opencode's own help labels its flag '(dangerous!)'. AGENTS.md's control invariant sanctions 'auto-resolves, DENIES, or kills-and-reclaims': deny is explicitly listed, bypass is not. The two that shipped are a different category — --no-chrome stops a browser attaching to a session nobody watches, and --pure makes a turn reproducible from the plan alone rather than from whatever plugins the operator happens to have installed. Encoding the refusals as tests rather than omissions means they cannot be silently re-added.

decision: TestResumeSendsSentinelOnSpawn (internal/provider/claudesession) is load-sensitive: it failed once under full-suite parallel load and passed 4/4 in isolation, including on a branch WITHOUT the change under test.
why: Recorded rather than fixed because I verified it is not mine before moving on — the same discipline that caught my WRONG 'pre-existing flake' call on the Windows store.Open failure earlier. There the evidence refuted me; here it supports the call: the test passes on a clean branch and the change under test only builds an argv, which cannot affect a session sentinel's timing. Worth fixing on its own terms (a timing-dependent test that only fails under load is a latent CI flake), but not by weakening it as a ride-along on an unrelated PR.

decision: Calibrations are CONTENT-ADDRESSED (id derived from the measurement identity, excluding capabilities/evidence) and a conflicting remeasurement returns ErrCalibrationConflict rather than overwriting. Attempts are stored per repetition, returned in run order, duplicates refused.
why: A calibration is a record of an OBSERVATION, not configuration. Content addressing makes re-probing idempotent — without it every probe accumulates a row and no lookup ever hits. Capabilities and evidence are excluded from the address because they are what was observed rather than what was observed ABOUT: including them would mint a new id whenever a probe's evidence differed by a timestamp. The conflict refusal is the sharper property: tasks bind to a calibration id to document what they ran on, so silently replacing the row when a binary is upgraded would retroactively rewrite history, leaving every already-bound task claiming a version that did not exist when it ran. Per-repetition attempts exist because agreement ACROSS repetitions is the calibration signal — a collapsed row cannot express it — and a duplicate repetition would double-count one result when runs are compared.

decision: Path containment refuses every ROOTED SHAPE on every platform (leading slash or backslash, drive-letter prefix including the drive-relative C:x form, both UNC spellings) rather than relying on filepath.IsAbs.
why: Windows CI caught a real gap, not a test artifact. filepath.IsAbs is platform-specific: on Windows '\\etc\\passwd' is NOT absolute (no drive) and on Unix 'C:\\Windows' is NOT absolute either, so one IsAbs check refuses a string on one platform and admits the identical string on the other. Four of six rooted shapes were admitted on darwin. This matters because a declared path is operator-supplied TEXT that may have been authored on a different OS than the one running it — the plan is portable even when the check was not. The test that exposed it was wrong the same way: it built its input with filepath.Join(Separator,...), which on Windows produces exactly the root-relative form IsAbs calls relative, so it asserted the wrong thing on the one platform where the distinction matters. General rule: for operator-supplied paths, never let a platform-conditional stdlib predicate be the whole security check.

decision: TestDeclarativeProgressRenewsStallButTotalDeadlineStillWins is the SECOND load-sensitive timing test found (after TestResumeSendsSentinelOnSpawn). Both fail only under full-suite parallel load and pass in isolation. Filed as a pattern, not two isolated flakes.
why: Verified not mine before recording: the docs branch changes only docs/guides/plan-format.md and internal/plan/docs_example_test.go — it cannot affect provider turn timing — and the test passed 3/3 in isolation on that same branch. Two independent timing tests failing the same way under load is a PATTERN worth naming: these tests assert which of two racing deadlines fires first, and under parallel load the machine's scheduling decides that rather than the code. A test whose result depends on how busy the host is will eventually fail in CI on an unrelated PR and send someone hunting a bug that is not there — which is precisely the cost I paid twice today. Worth fixing on their own terms (inject a clock, or widen the margin between the two deadlines so scheduling cannot invert them), NOT by weakening them as a ride-along on an unrelated PR.

decision: A doc page describing unmerged behavior is based on the branch that ships it, not on main. docs/design/plan-adaptive-concurrency.md sits on feat/output-reservations (#239), stacked on the 6-7-8 chain.
why: I nearly published it on main, then checked: the page describes ReadyPartitions, project-scoped reservations, path canonicalization, and worker-vs-task accounting — grep confirmed NONE of those exist on main, they are in #225/#228/#229. Publishing there would have documented features that do not exist, which is worse than no page because a reader trusts the docs over the code. General rule adopted: before publishing design docs for in-flight work, grep main for the identifiers the page names; if they are absent, the page belongs on the branch that adds them. Same discipline as the plan-format guide, where I split fields by ENFORCED vs merely PARSED rather than listing all of them as working.

decision: init resolves projects via ensureProjectKnown and config via vconfig.ConfigSource; it no longer imports store. #204 criterion 1 closed. Remaining CLI store readers: desktop_launch.go (real debt), supervisor_cmd.go + binding_resolver.go (supervisor-side, permanent).
why: init was the last CLI command opening the store, making the client a second writer to a supervisor-owned database. The self-verifying boundary gate PROVED the fix rather than being told about it: removing the import made TestOperatorClientsDoNotImportStore fail with 'init_cmd.go no longer imports store — delete its entry'. That is the design working — paying a debt forces removing the exemption, so the file cannot silently stay ungated against a later regression. Reusing ensureProjectKnown rather than re-implementing the fingerprint/ProjectEnsure dance means init and every other command agree on what 'this directory's project' is.

decision: The IPC drive surface has TWO command lists that must both be updated: the allow-list in handleConn's switch AND the dispatch switch in dispatchDrive.
why: I added the config commands to dispatchDrive only, and they were rejected as 'unknown command' before reaching it — a failure that reads like a missing handler when the handler exists. Found by a test, not by reading. Worth recording because the two lists are ~100 lines apart and nothing links them; the next person adding a drive command will hit the same thing.

decision: An ipc.Client is ONE request per connection. A caller making several calls must dial per call, not hold a client.
why: The protocol is deliberately dial->request->response->close (documented at internal/ipc/server.go's per-connection bounds). My config source held one client across the several calls config resolution makes and got 'broken pipe' on the second. Fixed by dialing per call, with the reason in a comment so it is not 'optimized' back into a held client — the held version works for exactly one call, which is the worst kind of wrong since it passes a smoke test.

decision: Full worktree reconciliation 2026-07-28: 23 worktrees -> 13, all 13 current with main (behind_main=0). GitHub is the source of truth; Gitea is a no-CI backup mirror (user confirmed).
why: Ten worktrees held branches whose PRs had already merged. Absorption was proven two ways rather than assumed: `git merge-tree --write-tree github/main <branch>` equal to main's tree proves a no-op merge (found 4), and for squash-merged branches whose patch-ids no longer match, checking that each branch's KEY ARTIFACT exists on main (found 6) — the raw diff is misleading there because it is dominated by deletions showing main is AHEAD, not that the branch has unlanded work. Every deletion was cross-checked against a MERGED PR number first. Three remote deletes 'failed' with 'remote ref does not exist', which is GitHub's auto-delete-on-merge having already removed them, not an error. The stacked chain (225->228->229->239) was rebuilt bottom-up by cherry-picking each branch's unique commits onto its rebuilt parent, since rebasing replays commits already in the new base.

decision: Remotes renamed so the DEFAULT is the source of truth: origin=GitHub (git@github.com:jbcom/radioactive-ralph.git), gitea=the no-CI backup mirror. Confirmed by the user: GitHub is authoritative, Gitea mirrors FROM it.
why: origin previously pointed at Gitea, so an unqualified `git push`/`git pull`/`gh` targeted the MIRROR. Every push this session named `github` explicitly, but a script or a moment of inattention would have written to the backup instead of the source. Direction was verified EMPIRICALLY before renaming rather than assumed: Gitea's main matched GitHub exactly, it held no branches GitHub lacked, and — decisively — it had ALREADY dropped the ten branches deleted from GitHub minutes earlier. Only a pull mirror does that; a push-mirror or independent remote would have retained them. All 13 worktrees share the repository's remote config, so the rename applies everywhere at once, and git rewrote every branch's upstream to origin/* automatically. Verified with `git push --dry-run` from both the primary checkout and a worktree.

decision: ProjectEnsureArgs.ResolveOnly resolves a directory to a project WITHOUT writing — skipping the accumulate/touch writes on the found path as well as the create on the miss path. desktop_launch.go uses it; no CLI file reads the store now.
why: A file-manager launch has an arbitrary working directory, often not a repo and sometimes '/', so plain project-ensure's create-on-miss would register that directory as a durable, operator-visible project just because someone double-clicked an icon. Skipping only the CREATE would not have been enough: the found path also ran AddProjectIdentifiers and TouchProjectLastSeen, so a 'resolve' would still mutate rows for a directory the operator never meant to register. Non-creation is proven by re-resolving the same fingerprint and asserting it is still unknown — that asserts the thing that would actually break, unlike counting rows. Every failure in the path is non-fatal by design (no supervisor, unreadable cwd, unknown directory all mean 'no project scope', which the GUI renders with a banner) because refusing to launch would leave a double-clicked icon doing nothing at all.

decision: Capability requirements use a CLOSED vocabulary derived from BindingConfig fields, not an open string set and not a per-provider table
why: An open vocabulary makes `requires` unfalsifiable: a key no binding can satisfy blocks every task forever, and a key none can fail is decoration. Deriving from BindingConfig (native_fanout, supports_resume, use_append_system_prompt) means the keys cannot drift from what a binding actually declares — a second table would diverge the first time a provider gained or lost a capability.
resolves: ralph-task `requires` parsed and persisted with zero consumers; a task needing native fan-out ran silently on a binding that cannot fan out

decision: An unrecognized capability key blocks the task, reported as ErrCapabilityUnknown distinct from ErrCapabilityUnmet
why: An unmet requirement is a scheduling fact an operator resolves by choosing another binding. An unknown key is a plan defect that NO binding can ever satisfy, so silently ignoring it would dispatch the task to a provider chosen by accident — the exact failure `requires` exists to prevent. Distinct sentinels let a caller tell 'pick a different provider' from 'fix the plan'.
resolves: typo in a requires list would have passed straight through

decision: The capability check runs in stepGateBlocks (before session/worker/slot allocation), not inside the runner
why: By the time a turn starts, a session row, a worker row, and a dispatch slot have all been committed to a task that can never succeed on this binding. Checking at the gate keeps that capacity available to tasks that can actually run, and matches where the approval gate already sits. Binding resolution uses BindingProbe so the check does not consume a provider-pool cursor.

decision: task_metadata rows are written as part of materializing a task, and the duplicate is a typed store error
why: Nothing in production ever wrote a task_metadata row — PutTaskMetadata had zero non-test callers. MarkBlockedCapability and MarkBlockedInput both record their reason there and fail closed without it, so BOTH were unreachable for every dispatch-materialized task; #228 depends on the same primitive. A task that cannot record why it is blocked is not fully materialized. The benign concurrent-dispatcher duplicate is typed (ErrDuplicateTaskMetadata) rather than matched on SQLite's error text, which would couple every caller to the driver's wording.
resolves: latent: MarkBlockedCapability/MarkBlockedInput would have errored for any task not created by ImportPlan

decision: The plan-format guide's capability section is anchored by tests that EXTRACT the example from the guide and diff the documented key table against the enforced set
why: A restated copy in the test lets the guide drift into documenting a shape the parser rejects, and the guide is what an operator actually writes a plan from. The key-table check runs in both directions: a key enforced but undocumented, and a key documented but unenforced (which would block every step using it).

decision: Review findings are verified against the code BEFORE being accepted or refused, and every fix carries a negative proof (revert it, confirm the named test fails for the stated reason).
why: Across 24 findings on 8 PRs this pass, the split was roughly 20 real / 4 wrong-on-the-facts — and the wrong ones were plausible enough to have been 'fixed' on assertion. Two examples: a reported ids[0] panic was unreachable because Go's || short-circuits (proved with a recover() probe), and a claimed duplicate event WAS real but for the opposite reason I first grepped for. Verification also caught two cases where MY OWN prior fix had broken the thing it claimed to protect.
resolves: accepting or dismissing review findings on plausibility rather than evidence

decision: A transition check that guards an event emit belongs INSIDE the store transaction that performs the write, not in the caller.
why: PR #247: dispatch evaluates the capability gate more than once per pass (fan-out probe plus the per-step loop), so a caller comparing against a task row it read earlier sees a stale status. Computing 'was it already blocked?' in the orchestrator still emitted 4 events across 3 passes instead of 1; moving it into markMetadataBlocked's transaction made it exactly 1. MarkBlockedCapability/MarkBlockedInput now return whether they transitioned.

decision: A fail-closed block must be REVERSIBLE by the action it asks for. store.ClearTaskBlock releases a capability/input-blocked task back to pending when the requirement is satisfied.
why: ClaimTask accepts only pending or ready, so a blocked task stayed permanently unclaimable even after an operator performed the exact fix the block prompted — a trap, not a gate, and the plan never completed. Only the two fail-closed pre-dispatch states are cleared: running/done/failed belong to the worker lifecycle and resetting one would discard real execution state.

decision: Strict binding decides honorability by comparing against the RESOLVED model, never by inspecting the config's shape.
why: resolveModel treats SonnetModel as a UNIVERSAL fallback, so 'the binding has a mapping for this tier' and 'the binding ran this tier' are different claims. Shape-inference approved exactly the substitutions strict mode exists to refuse: a claude-type binding short-circuited to honorable for EVERY tier (strict opus ran sonnet while provenance claimed opus), and a non-tier model counted as mapped merely for being non-empty (strict gpt-4 ran gpt-5).

decision: A record whose whole purpose is COMPARISON must reject empty identity fields rather than storing a sentinel.
why: Calibration attempts are identified by output digest and agreement is computed by comparing them. NOT NULL accepts the empty string, so N failed runs all carried "" and matched each other — reading as unanimous agreement from runs that produced nothing, which is worse than no signal at all. Rejecting at write time beats teaching every comparison to special-case a sentinel.

decision: A flag that CHANGES an existing command's semantics ships behind a protocol version an older peer rejects, and the version test compares against a literal previous maximum rather than the current constant.
why: ProjectEnsure.ResolveOnly promises not to mutate; a supervisor predating it ignores the unknown field and runs the mutating path anyway, so a git-fingerprint resolve from a moved checkout records that path as the project's newest worker directory. Version skew is routine (desktop upgraded, long-lived supervisor not). Only the changed semantic carries the higher floor so rolling upgrades still work. The literal matters: comparing against ProtoVersion, which the same change bumps, would make the assertion vacuous forever.

decision: Design docs state what SHIPPED, and name unimplemented intent as open work; where a doc overclaimed, the gap is filed as an issue rather than only reworded.
why: Three docs claimed guarantees main does not provide: total task ordering (import never sets sequence_ordinal for parallel steps), completion owner-guarding (VerifyAndComplete reads the CURRENT owner, so worker A's late result is written under worker B's session — filed as #248), and output-escape detection (no completion-time check reads declared outputs at all). Overclaiming in a design doc is worse than silence: the next reader builds on a guarantee that is not there. Slot-saturation silence filed as #249.

decision: Provider write containment is KERNEL-enforced (macOS sandbox-exec), opt-in per agent.Start via ContainmentRoot rather than derived from Dir, and fails closed on unsupported platforms.
why: secureProjectPath validates strings inside Ralph's own process; the provider is a separate process opening by pathname minutes later, and no string Ralph returns reaches its syscalls. Only the kernel can refuse the write. Opt-in because 'where a process starts' is not the same claim as 'the only place it may write', and conflating them would change every existing caller. Fails closed because a caller that believes it is contained when it is not makes exactly the false guarantee this replaces. Seatbelt's inheritance into spawned processes is load-bearing, not incidental: a fan-out provider runs sub-agents, so a top-level-only boundary would be escaped by the very providers Ralph runs.

decision: The containment profile grants NO temp directory, and a regression test asserts every writable subpath resolves to the containment root.
why: The draft granted the resolved TMPDIR so scratch files would work. On macOS TMPDIR resolves under /private/tmp, so that one line allowed writes to a subtree holding other tools' and other users' files WHILE THE POLICY STILL REPORTED CONTAINMENT. The behavioral test caught it — the escape target wrote successfully. A convenience grant that widens the boundary is worse than no containment because it reports success. The regression test inspects the PROFILE's grants rather than scanning argv: in tests the root itself lives under a temp dir, so a substring scan cannot distinguish the intended grant from an extra one.

decision: The Seatbelt profile allows by default and denies WRITES only, rather than default-deny.
why: Default-deny would have to enumerate every read, mach lookup, and network call each provider CLI needs — an open-ended list differing per provider and per version, whose first omission surfaces as a provider bug rather than a policy one. The guarantee is scoped to writes, so the profile denies exactly that; reads stay covered by the validation layer and network egress is explicitly out of scope.

decision: Native Windows write containment is CLOSED as not-needed rather than left open as a gap.
why: No provider can run on native Windows at all — agent.Start allocates a pty through creack/pty which returns ErrPTYUnsupported, and the Windows SCM safety spec states it directly: 'Native Windows provider workers are already unsupported'. Windows operators run under WSL, which is Linux, so Linux containment covers them. Building a Windows primitive would guard a code path that cannot execute, and this repo treats dead code as a defect. A test records the reasoning and fails if Available() ever reports true on Windows, asserting the CONTRACT rather than the platform so it stays meaningful if a provider path is ever added.

decision: Linux containment must use a RE-EXEC helper (restrict, then syscall.Exec immediately), never an in-process landlock_restrict_self call from Go.
why: MEASURED on kernel 6.12 / Landlock ABI 6: LANDLOCK_RESTRICT_SELF_TSYNC (all-thread enforcement) requires ABI 8, and below that restrict_self binds only the CALLING THREAD. A thread created BEFORE the call writes outside the root successfully. Go's runtime has threads running before any user code executes, so an in-process call would ship a boundary with a hole — the same 'reports success while not containing' failure as the macOS TMPDIR grant. Exec replaces the process image with a single thread and the domain IS inherited across execve, so nothing survives but the restriction.

decision: Linux write containment ships via Landlock behind a RE-EXEC helper, and the handled-rights mask handles ONLY mutating rights (never EXECUTE/READ_FILE/READ_DIR/IOCTL_DEV).
why: Landlock denies a HANDLED right everywhere no rule grants it. A mask written as 'all write bits' (0x7fe) silently handles bit 2 READ_FILE and bit 3 READ_DIR, so granting them only under the root made every file outside unreadable — including the provider binary and the dynamic loader — and execve failed with EACCES, a symptom that points at exec permissions and says nothing about reads. Root-caused by stuck-loop-debugger after several failed cycles. Three tests now guard the mask itself rather than only end-to-end: no read/exec right handled, nothing outside the ABI's defined bits (an undefined bit makes create_ruleset EINVAL), and every mutating right covered since one left out is a hole.

decision: Containment behavioral tests build a REAL helper binary instead of re-execing the go test binary.
why: On Linux, Wrap re-execs the CALLING binary as a containment helper. Under `go test` that is the test binary, which has no MaybeRunHelper in main(), so it rejects the sentinel and NEVER RUNS THE COMMAND — and every 'did the file appear?' assertion then reads the absent file as successful containment. This false pass was OBSERVED before being fixed. It is the same trap as the macOS TMPDIR grant: a test that reports containment it never demonstrated is worse than no test.

decision: Increment boundaries and salvage from plan_graph.go / task_metadata_view.go, verified against archive/plan-v2-dag rather than assumed. (1) ErrTaskNotRunning moves from plan_graph.go:197 to internal/store/tasks.go, beside the ErrTaskNotOwnedRunning that already wraps it at tasks.go:563; same package, no import cycle, and the graph it names lives in task_deps which tasks.go owns. (2) enrichTaskMetadata is discarded — its ONLY callers are tasks.go GetTask (:408) and ListTasks (:460), the exact hot-path widening being rejected. (3) TeamRollups/TeamRollup are NOT discarded despite living in the same task_metadata_view.go: they are consumed by supervisor.go:349 and the GUI team view (gui/team.go, views.go:262), so they move to internal/store/task_metadata.go. (4) Keep main's isSQLiteBusy from PR #212, not the archive's: the archive matches only sqliteBusyCode (5), while main's also handles SQLITE_LOCKED (6) and keeps a message fallback for errors that lost their type across a boundary.
why: The design named plan_graph.go and task_metadata_view.go as discards. Discarding either file wholesale would have deleted live functionality — ErrTaskNotRunning breaks the build, and TeamRollups breaks the supervisor status path plus the GUI team view. Grepping the actual callers before deleting is the difference between a refactor and a regression. The isSQLiteBusy comparison also runs the other way from the usual salvage direction: the code already on main is broader than the archive's, so the archive version must not overwrite it.

decision: The four CLI invocation changes in archive/plan-v2-dag are NOT part of the DAG feature and are classified separately. TAKE: codex `-c model_reasoning_effort=%q` and the model/effort plumbing through invocation.Model/invocation.Effort — that is the exact-invocation-identity work, additive and behind StrictBinding. DEFER to its own PR with real-CLI verification: claude `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` and `--no-chrome`, and opencode `--pure --auto`. DISCARD: the defaultOpencodeProvider NativeFanout true->false flip.
why: bypassPermissions is a security posture change, not an invocation detail: it disables claude's permission prompting for every turn Ralph runs. It may well be correct for a supervised non-interactive runtime — main's claude.go:122 already treats a permission prompt as a KILL condition, so prompting is useless there — but that argument deserves its own PR and its own decision record, not a silent ride-along in a DAG branch. --no-chrome and --pure --auto are likewise real behavior changes to installed CLIs whose flags must be verified against the actual binaries, which unit tests with fake shell scripts cannot do. The NativeFanout flip is a straight regression: main documents opencode NativeFanout:true as 'verified against the installed opencode 1.18.3', while the archive downgrades it to false pending a calibration fixture that does not exist yet — losing a proven capability to satisfy a process that was never built.

subject: fix(provider): separate turn deadlines from stall detection and contain provider process trees (#209)

decision: Busy-retry loops around SQLite operations are thin backstops (3 attempts, 20ms step), never a second timeout. The DSN's busy_timeout(5000) is the primary wait; a retry loop layered on top of it multiplies the total rather than bounding it.
why: PR #212 added 20-attempt loops with an increasing 25ms backoff to ensureJournalModeWAL and applyMigrationWithRetry — 5.25s each, and both run at EVERY store.Open, so one contended Open could burn over 10s of backoff on top of the 5s busy_timeout SQLite already spends blocking for the lock. TestRun_SecondRunRefuses opens three stores against a 15s shutdown bound and timed out on Windows CI. I initially and incorrectly reported that failure as a pre-existing named-pipe flake, citing the test file's own comments about historical Windows flakiness; the evidence refuted that (main green, PR #209 zero failures across ten runs, both failures on the one PR touching store.Open). The retries only need to cover the handoff immediately after a concurrent first-opener commits, because the winner's WAL switch and user_version bump are both persistent — a loser needs one or two quick re-reads. 240ms per Open instead of 10.5s, with the concurrency reproducers still passing at -count=5.

decision: Any JSON that carries a safety-relevant contract must be scanned for duplicate keys BEFORE decoding, via a token-stream walk that refuses a repeat at any nesting depth. encoding/json silently keeps the LAST value for a repeated key even under DisallowUnknownFields, and a map decode cannot detect the duplicate because it has already collapsed the pair.
why: Found by review on PR #217 and reproduced before fixing. The plan grammar's ordering guarantee was defeated outright: {"id":"x","after":["prepare"],"after":[]} parsed to ids=[] stated=true — an unconditioned root that would dispatch BEFORE the task it declares a dependency on. The second half is worse in kind: {"after":null,"after":[]} sailed past rejectNullMetadataFields, because that check unmarshals into map[string]json.RawMessage and the duplicate was already gone by then. So a validator built on a map decode cannot police duplicates no matter how strict it looks. This generalizes past the plan grammar to any config or manifest where a repeated key changes behavior rather than just the value.

decision: Task Description stays OUT of the default operator snapshot and comes instead from an explicit, opt-in per-task detail query. The TUI/GUI request it only for the one task an operator has drilled into, never for a whole list.
why: I first tried simply restoring Description to the snapshot DTO because the TUI meso/micro views and the GUI taskLabel had all silently degraded to bare task IDs, and two e2e tests fail without it. The privacy tests refuted that: TestReadOperatorSnapshotProjectIsolationFanoutAndContentSafety seeds a task description of "/private/repository/source-plan.md" and asserts the snapshot JSON never contains it. That test is deliberate, not incidental — the branch author put "description" on the forbidden list precisely because Description is orch's step.Text, author-controlled free text that can carry filesystem paths, URLs, or secrets, and issue #204 forbids exposing repository paths. Widening the always-on snapshot would leak it for every task in every list, to every observer, forever. But the issue says 'DEFAULT operator DTOs must not expose' and separately allows exposure for legitimate follow-up, so the resolution is scope rather than omission: a detail query the operator explicitly issues for a single drilled-into task. That keeps the bulk snapshot content-free while giving the human-facing views the label they need to be usable at all.

decision: Project initialization and plan listing move behind supervisor IPC commands rather than keeping a client-side store.Open bootstrap exception. Three groups are needed: project resolve/create/touch/add-identifiers (init_cmd + client.go), project config apply (init_cmd), and plan list/create/set-status (plan_cmd). `plan ls` gains --json in the same pass since it is the same command surface.
why: AGENTS.md line 21-22 already settles the design question I was about to treat as open: the dumb client 'connects to the supervisor via its socket, initializes project config, and renders a read-only view. It refuses to run without a supervisor.' So there is no legitimate pre-supervisor bootstrap window for --init to exploit — project initialization is supervisor-mediated by contract, and the current store.Open in init_cmd.go/client.go/plan_cmd.go is a violation rather than a necessary exception. That also rules out the tempting shortcut of adding a read-only query and leaving the writes alone: ResolveProject/CreateProject/AddProjectIdentifiers/ApplyProjectConfig/CreatePlan/SetPlanStatus are all writes, so this needs drive commands, not observe queries.

decision: CI readiness probes must key on a marker the privacy contract permits, and changing a client's user-visible output requires grepping the workflows for that string. The supervisor-readiness probe now matches 'captured_at=' from the safe snapshot line instead of 'supervisor is up (pid N, ...)'.
why: PR #219 correctly removed the PID from the client's status output — PID is on issue #204's forbidden list — but three CI greps (two bash, one PowerShell) still asserted the old string. The failure mode was actively misleading: the smoke test looped 30 times and reported 'supervisor never became ready' while the log printed immediately above it showed 'supervisor listening socket=... pid=...'. Nothing was wrong with the supervisor; the probe was asserting a string the binary no longer prints. Verified the replacement against a real binary rather than by inspection: no supervisor still fails cleanly, and a live one yields 'project=... plans=0 tasks=0 active_workers=0 captured_at=...'.

decision: CI gets one-in-flight-per-PR concurrency with main EXCLUDED from cancellation (group falls back to github.run_id, cancel-in-progress only on pull_request).
why: ci.yml had no concurrency group at all, so every push started a full run — four macOS jobs among them — while superseded runs kept their queued slots. Measured: one branch held EIGHT queued CI runs, seven obsolete, occupying 28 macOS jobs for work that no longer existed. Four of 25 required checks are macOS-only, so that contention was blocking all 17 open PRs. main is excluded because its runs gate releases and cancelling them would be worse than the starvation being fixed; run_id gives each main run a unique group so collision is impossible. codeql.yml and release.yml already used this pattern — adopted rather than invented.
resolves: macOS runner starvation from superseded PR runs

decision: A CI watcher must assert on the SPECIFIC condition it claims to detect, not on any state change.
why: The macOS-availability watcher reported 'macOS COMPLETED: cancelled' — it matched a run I had deliberately cancelled to test #252, not a runner actually starting. Same class of false positive as the containment tests that read an absent file as successful containment: a check that passes for the wrong reason is worse than no check, because it ends the wait early.

decision: The macOS CI starvation is GitHub-side capacity, and #252 (CI concurrency) cannot unblock it on its own because it is itself blocked by the checks it fixes.
why: Ruled out every repo-side cause by verification rather than assumption: both runner labels (macos-latest, macos-15-intel) are current per actions/runner-images; the repo is PUBLIC so macOS minutes are free and unmetered; githubstatus reports operational; actionlint is clean and every non-macOS job on the same runs passes. #252 removes real self-inflicted contention (28 macOS jobs held by superseded runs on one branch) but only governs its own branch until merged, and it cannot merge because four macOS-only checks are in the required set. enforce_admins=true, and --admin/force-merge past red CI are forbidden by standing rules, so this is a genuine external wait rather than a decision to make.

decision: macOS CI starvation is conclusively GitHub-side capacity, proven by draining the queue to near-zero rather than by elimination alone.
why: Ruling causes out one at a time still left 'contention' as a plausible explanation, and #252 could not test it because a concurrency block only governs its own branch. So I cancelled ~28 obsolete queued runs across every branch manually: repo-wide CI queue went 11 -> 3 live runs, freeing 100+ macOS job slots. macOS jobs on the remaining runs STAYED QUEUED. A repo holding almost no backlog still cannot start a macOS job, which is a positive demonstration rather than an inference. #252 remains correct — it stops the backlog rebuilding on every push — but was never going to be sufficient on its own.

decision: Platform-specific code is verified by BUILDING AND LINTING for every target arch/OS it claims to support, not by testing on the development machine.
why: PR #251 shipped two failures from single-platform verification in one session. (1) syscall.O_PATH is defined on linux/arm64 but NOT linux/amd64 — the Docker verification host is arm64, so go build, go vet, and the full Linux test suite passed while amd64 CI could not compile the package; fixed by using golang.org/x/sys/unix, which defines it uniformly. (2) golangci-lint on darwin never evaluates the linux build tag, so four gosec findings in contain_linux.go were invisible locally and would have failed CI's Lint job. The check that actually holds is `GOOS=linux GOARCH=<each> go build` plus `GOOS=linux golangci-lint run`, since one extra arch would not have caught the first case either.

decision: Deliberately yielded the CI queue to #252 by cancelling every other branch's queued run, so the concurrency fix can land first.
why: The macOS backlog REBUILDS on every push, and #252 is the only change that stops it — but a concurrency block governs only the branch carrying it, so until #252 is on main every update-branch and push re-creates the starvation. Confirmed empirically: after the first hand-drain the queue climbed back to 8 purely from my own pushes and rebases. Serializing on #252 costs the other branches one CI cycle and removes the cause. The cancelled runs are NOT failures; they are re-triggered after #252 merges.

decision: A `providers` restriction is a PER-TICK admission refusal (worker.admission_refused), not a durable blocked_capability; `requires` remains a durable block.
why: They are not the same class of refusal, though my original commit said they were. `providers` names operator CONFIGURATION — binding the project to an allowed provider fixes it — so a durable block would leave an operator clearing a state their config edit already resolved. `requires` is durable because no configuration change makes a provider gain a capability it lacks. Surfaced by CodeRabbit's P1 on #250, which also showed the gate could not decide `providers` at all: BindingProbe deliberately does not advance a pool cursor, so it only saw the pool HEAD and blocked codex-only tasks on a [claude,codex] pool. Now resolved at dispatch with bounded pool rotation.

decision: Containment refuses a root that is not a directory, and the containment feature is wired through to the runners with a WIRING test distinct from the behavioral ones.
why: Two defects in my own containment work, both found by review. NewPolicy accepted a regular file (EvalSymlinks resolves one happily), yielding a policy whose 'root' is a single file — macOS would build a subpath rule for a non-directory and Landlock would grant directory-creation rights beneath a plain file; neither is a boundary anyone reasoned about. Worse, ContainmentRoot had ZERO production callers: internal/contain's behavioral tests proved the kernel refuses escaping writes while no real turn was ever confined, and the well-tested lower layer is exactly what made it look wired up. Behavioral tests cannot see the wiring layer, so it needs its own test.

decision: scripts/verify-repo-claims.sh checks in-flight repo claims against GitHub and the working trees, and is run BEFORE asserting status rather than after.
why: Every wrong thing this session was a check that passed for the wrong reason: a containment test reading an absent file as containment, a watcher matching a run I had cancelled myself, a test whose fixture never reached the code path, and a merge driver whose static open-count could not distinguish 'waiting on CI' from 'wedged'. Self-reported status has the same failure mode. On its first run the verifier immediately found an unresolved review thread and uncommitted files I had not noticed.
resolves: status claims asserted from memory rather than from the source of truth

decision: A background driver must report WHY it is not progressing, and exit when something needs a decision, rather than printing a progress counter.
why: The first merge driver printed only an open-PR count. It sat at 9 for several rounds, which looks identical whether CI is merely slow, a PR has a conflict, or tests are failing. Replacing it with one that reports blocked/behind/ready/DIRTY/FAILING per round surfaced a real test failure on #245 within two rounds — 'no supervisor listening', because a CI step ran --init before starting a supervisor, which only ever worked because init used to be a store writer. The old driver would have shown the same static 9.

decision: A workflow-level pattern is verified against EACH workflow's triggers before being applied, not copied across them.
why: I added the same concurrency block to ci.yml, service-managers.yml and provider-live.yml. Only ci.yml is pull_request-triggered; the other two are workflow_dispatch-only, so github.event.pull_request.number is always empty and the run_id fallback gave every run a unique group — a concurrency block that could never cancel anything, carrying a comment claiming it did. Dispatch-only workflows are keyed on github.ref instead.

subject: docs(state): #248 closed via #256; #249 split out as its own item

decision: Evidence is attributed to the REPORTING session, and both the mark AND the event are suppressed when that session no longer owns the task.
why: store.MarkDone/MarkFailed are owner-guarded against the session they are GIVEN, and the only caller handed them the CURRENT owner — so a reaped worker's late result was written under its replacement's session, the guard passed, and the replacement's attempt was silently overwritten (#248). Fixing the mark was not enough: worker.verification_failed still fired unconditionally, so a stale rejection announced a failure against an attempt still running. A correct store plus a lying event stream is worse than either alone, because an operator reads the event, not the row.

decision: InvocationConfigHash guarantees only that EQUAL hashes mean the same configured invocation; unequal hashes mean 'not known to be the same'.
why: Changing only the binding alias changes the hash while the runners build an identical argv, so 'different hashes ran different command lines' was false in exactly that case. The asymmetry is deliberate rather than a defect: the hash keys a measurement of an ALIAS, and an operator who splits one binding into two has created two things to calibrate independently even where today's argv coincides — the aliases exist so they can diverge. Treating them as interchangeable would attribute one alias's evidence to another.

decision: dispatch.saturated reports how many ready candidates went UNEXAMINED, emitted on the transition into saturation only.
why: Every other admission gate reported itself while slot saturation returned 0,nil silently — byte-identical to an empty ready set. Those are the two states most worth distinguishing: 'waiting on dependencies' clears itself, 'ready work, no capacity' may never clear if a worker is wedged. The candidate count is what makes it actionable; 'a slot was unavailable' is nearly as uninformative as silence. Transition-only per #247, with releaseDispatchSlot re-arming it, or it appends an identical event every tick.

decision: The observe surface classifies a blocked task from its DURABLE STATUS (BlockedSummary: capability|input|approval + static remediation text), never by forwarding the stored blocked_reason string.
why: internal/observe's contract is that raw payload text never crosses the boundary — FailureCategory says so outright. Forwarding blocked_reason made it the one field leaking unbounded error-derived text. The right fix was a classification, not truncation; and because the status already carries the classification, the per-plan reason join disappeared entirely. That removed three further findings at once: a cross-plan key collision (per-plan maps flattened into one keyed by TASK ID, and ids are plan-local and positional, so plan A's block appeared on plan B's healthy task), an N+1/page-scope mismatch, and a read outside the snapshot transaction. store.ListTaskBlockingReasons was deleted — a bulk query defended by three separate correctness arguments was evidence the join was wrong, not that it needed better guards.

decision: StateForTask maps blocked_capability and blocked_input to InputRequired alongside blocked and ready_pending_approval.
why: Both were unmapped and StateForTask's default FAILS the whole projection, so a single fail-closed blocked task returned 'unknown Ralph task status' for the entire snapshot — hiding every plan, task and worker. The status that exists to make a stall visible instead blanked the operator's whole view. Found only because a test for the blocking classification put such a task into a snapshot fixture; reading the code would not have surfaced it.

decision: contain_provider_writes is a project config key; absent OR malformed means OFF.
why: Containment was code-only via WithProviderWriteContainment, so an operator could not enable it without a rebuild. Absent means off because enabling changes what a provider may do — one legitimately writing to a shared cache outside the checkout starts failing — so it is an operator decision, not an upgrade side effect. MALFORMED also means off, deliberately: a typo must not silently ENABLE a boundary that makes writes fail, because the symptom would be unexplained provider errors far from the cause. Both bool and string are accepted since a store layer round-trips values as JSON strings.
